chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
title: Parker's 'Lover Man' night and the Casablanca crowd
summary: A night when Parker's 'Lover Man' chorus left no one willing to play, plus local singers and Kenny Bright.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: You probably remember the recording that Charlie Parker made on "Lover Man." Well, I knew what inspired that particular recording. One night we were all in the Casablanca, and he played "Lover Man," and he played so great on "Lover Man" until when he finished his chorus, no other horn player put a horn to his mouth. And the time just kept going on... And he looked up and smiled, and put his horn back in his mouth and kept on playing, you know. It was classic. It was classic, you know. Nobody had to play. Oh, I heard him play some... On the bandstand that night was Roy Porter, Curtis Counce, the bassist, and Jimmy Bunn, the pianist, who eventually made the recording with him when he was sick from his nervous breakdown later on.

But anyway, I saw a lot of great moments at the Casablanca Club. A lot of great singers were around. They had a singer around here named Bing Richman(?), they called him "The Black Bing." Great baritone singer. And Pha Terrell from Andy Kirk's great band, he had been around. In fact, this was where he died, was in Los Angeles. They had a lot of great talent. Charlie Fox out of St. Louis... All kinds of guys were around during that time. The trumpet player out of Detroit, Willie Wells, and another trumpet player who used to hang out with us quite a bit during that time, Kenny Bright. I know you remember good old Kenny Bright! [LAUGHS]

Yeah. He would be on the scene, yeah. He wasn't a very good soloist, but academically he was good, and he would write the little arrangements in the head, you know, that the guys would play and what have you. He just wanted to be on the scene, you know.
